Atomic level explorer

Energy levels and radiative lifetimes for 104 spectra, computed from NIST ASD transition probabilities. Levels whose lifetime falls between 1 and 1000 ps are marked throughout. Sources and method are listed at the foot of the page.

Levels in view

ConfigurationTermJ Energy eVLifetime Strongest decay eVParity

Every chain below starts on a level that holds population, climbs in hops of 2 or 3 photons of one colour, and lands on a real level. Each hop matches a measured level gap to within the stated detuning, obeys the parity rule for that photon number, and obeys |ΔJ| ≤ m. Every rung except the last outlives the intra-burst pulse spacing of 20 ps, so the next pulse arrives at an occupied level.

Top state is the axis to read first. A chain ending above the ionization limit lands on an autoionizing resonance: intrinsically fast, but it decays by throwing out an electron, so the ladder ends in an ion rather than a photon. A chain ending on a bound level with a picosecond lifetime ends in EUV light instead, and the emitted wavelength is given. Those exist only in ions — ionizing once roughly doubles the ionization limit while the level structure keeps its shape, so states that autoionize in the neutral sit safely below the limit one step up the isoelectronic sequence.

Rung
a real level the ladder stops on — one per arrow, plus the state it starts from.
Pattern / order
photons absorbed at each hop, and their sum. 3+3 is order 6.
Energy match
how far a level gap sits from the photon energy that has to bridge it. Under 25 meV closes on driver tuning alone; the search allows 150 meV, which is roughly the chirp and AC Stark budget.
Hop strength
whether a hop is strong, which is a different question from whether it is allowed. A two-photon hop climbs through a virtual point, and its rate depends on how close real levels lie to that point; the estimate here is built from the one-photon oscillator strengths of the same atom and spans eight orders of magnitude, so it ranks hops rather than measuring them.
Lifetimes
computed as 1/ΣAki over the decay channels NIST lists, so a level whose channels are only partly covered reads as an upper bound. Deciding whether a rung holds population uses a conservative floor instead, τ k/n for k of n channels known. A rung marked unpublished has no A-value at all: below the ionization limit that almost always means far longer than 20 ps, but it is assumed rather than read.
Chance fits
how many levels fall inside one 150 meV window by accident. Fe I sits at 16 — aim anywhere and something is there, so an energy match proves nothing. Hg II sits at 0.7, where a match means something.

Sources

Energy levels and transition probabilities. NIST Atomic Spectra Database v5.12, retrieved 22 August 2026. Kramida A., Ralchenko Yu., Reader J. and NIST ASD Team (2024), doi:10.18434/T4W30F. Cross-checked against ExoMol LiDB — Owens A. et al. (2025), JQSRT 330, 109242 — which is itself derived from ASD, so not an independent check.

Lifetimes are not tabulated anywhere. They are computed here as τ = 1 / Σ Aki over every listed decay channel, J-resolved, and are upper bounds where a level’s channels are only partly covered. Levels above the first ionization limit autoionize and are left blank. Oscillator strengths come from the same A-values, f = 1.4992×10−16 (gk/gi) Aki λ2 with λ in ångström, and are one-photon quantities only. The Ladders tab is built by scripts/ladder.py from these same tables: hops of 2 or 3 photons of one colour out of 1030, 1060, 1550, 1600, 1900 and 2000 nm, matched to a measured level gap within 150 meV, parity and |ΔJ| ≤ m enforced per hop, and every rung but the last required to outlive a 20 ps intra-burst spacing. Hop amplitudes are perturbative dominant-term estimates built from the same oscillator strengths, so they rank hops and do not measure them, and no oscillator strength exists for the hop into the autoionizing region. Vapour temperatures belong to the neutral element, not to the ion, and are a precondition for preparing any charge state of it: the 1 Pa points (about 1014 cm−3) from the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 84th ed.; metals after Alcock, Itkin & Horrigan (1984).
